Puzzle: Here is an acute angle.

steps: The vertex A is at the centre of the protractor, so the units of 1 degree between two arms give the angle.
The long marks come every 10 units and the medium marks 5 units after each long mark, so we can count in 10s or in 5s.
∠KAL holds 3 long steps: 3 × 10° = 30°.
∠WAL holds 5 long steps: 5 × 10° = 50°.
∠TAK holds 12 long steps: 12 × 10° = 120°.
Check by counting in 5s: 6 × 5° = 30°, 10 × 5° = 50° and 24 × 5° = 120°, the same as the counts in 10s.
Place the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex H.
Turn the protractor until one arm lies along the 0 line, and read the scale that starts at that 0.
Follow the other arm out to the scale: the first figure reads 47°.
Do the same for the second figure: it reads 23°.
Do the same for the third figure: it reads 108°.
Check with a right angle (90°): 47° and 23° are less than 90°, and 108° is more than 90°.
Sample answer: choose a corner of the board and put the centre of the protractor exactly on that corner.
Turn the protractor until one edge lies along the 0 line, and read the scale that starts at that 0.
Follow the other edge out to the scale and read the number: the corner of a board or a book reads about 90°.
Do the same for the door and for a window: each gives its own reading, and a door opened a little reads less than 90°.
Put the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex H and turn it until the arm HI lies along the 0 line.
Read the scale where the arm HJ crosses it: the first angle is ∠IHJ = 42° and the second angle is ∠IHJ = 116°.
The paper protractor was made by folding a straight angle into 8 equal parts: 180 ÷ 8 gives 22.5, so its creases are at 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°, 112.5°, 135° and 157.5°.
42° lies between 22.5° and 45°, so it is not on a crease.
116° lies between 112.5° and 135°, so it is not on a crease.
Neither angle falls exactly on a crease, so the paper protractor cannot measure them.
Put the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex of the angle and turn it until one arm lies along the 0 line.
Read the scale that starts at that 0 where the other arm crosses it.
Do this for each of the six angles: a = 80°, b = 120°, c = 60°, d = 130°, e = 130° and f = 60°.
Check with a right angle (90°): a = 80°, c = 60° and f = 60° are less than 90°, and b = 120°, d = 130° and e = 130° are more than 90°.
Put the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex X and turn it until the arm XA lies along the 0 line.
Read the scale where the arm XB crosses it: ∠AXB = 65°.
Measure ∠BXE and ∠CXE in the same way: ∠BXE = 115° and ∠CXE = 85°.
Find ∠BXC by subtraction: ∠BXC = ∠BXE − ∠CXE = 115° − 85° = 30°.
Check: A, X and E lie on one line, so ∠AXB + ∠BXE = 65° + 115° = 180°.
Put the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex Q and turn it until the arm QP lies along the 0 line. All three angles share the arm QP, so one 0 line serves all three.
Read the scale where each arm crosses it: QR at 45°, QS at 100° and QT at 150°.
So ∠PQR = 45°, ∠PQS = 100° and ∠PQT = 150°.
Check the order: an arm further from QP must read a bigger number, and 45° < 100° < 150°.
A clock face is one full turn of 360°, cut by the 12 numbers into 12 equal gaps.
One gap is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees. At 1 o'clock the hands are 1 gap apart, so the angle is 1 × 30° = 30°.
At 2 o'clock the hands are 2 gaps apart: 2 × 30° = 60°.
At 4 o'clock the hands are 4 gaps apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.
At 6 o'clock the hands are 6 gaps apart: 6 × 30° = 180°.
Other hours work the same way: at 3 o'clock, 3 × 30° = 90°.
At 9 o'clock, 9 × 30° = 270° one way round, and the other way round is 360° − 270° = 90°.
The door turns about the place where it meets the wall, the hinge, and this place does not move.
The two lines that make the opening are the edge of the door and the wall, so they are the two arms.
Open the door wider: the opening between its edge and the wall grows, so the amount a door is open is an angle.
Check with the closed door: its edge lies along the wall, so there is no opening.
An angle shows a turn: one arm is where the turn starts and the other arm is where it ends, and the arms meet at the vertex.
Fix one arm at the position where the swing starts; it begins at the point where the swing hangs.
Watch how high the swing goes on one side before it comes back.
Draw the second arm from the hanging point to that highest position; the two arms make the angle.
Check with what Vidya noticed: the further back she starts, the greater the angle and the greater the speed.
Look at one slab: its slanting edge is one arm of an angle, and it can be seen on the toy.
The second arm starts at the top of the slab and goes straight across, level with the ground; this top horizontal ray is not drawn, so it is not visible. The two arms make an angle.
Compare two slabs: a gentle slab makes a small angle and a steeper slab makes a larger angle.
Check with the balls: the slab with the larger angle makes the ball roll faster, so a larger angle means a greater slope.
Sample answer: the horizontal line touching the insects is one arm of the angle.
Draw a line along the rotated insect; this line is the other arm.
The two arms meet at the point that does not move when the insect turns; this point of rotation on the line is the vertex, and the arc between the arms shows the amount of rotation.
Check by turning the insect back: the arc shrinks to nothing, because the two arms lie on each other.
Draw a base ray with its vertex at one end.
Place the centre of the protractor on the vertex and turn it until the base ray lies along the 0 line.
Read the scale that starts at 0 on the base ray, count up to the size needed and mark a point there. For 112°, go to 110° and then count 2 small marks more.
Join the mark to the vertex with a ruler. Do this for 110°, 40°, 75°, 112° and 134°.
Check by eye: 40° and 75° are less than 90°, so they look narrower than a square corner; 110°, 112° and 134° are more than 90°, so they look wider, and 134° is the widest.
Sample answer: join A to a grid point with a straight line; this line is the first arm of each angle, so every angle starts at A.
Acute angle: join A to a grid point so that the opening is smaller than a square corner, which is a right angle of 90°.
Obtuse angle: join A to a grid point so that the opening is wider than a square corner but narrower than a straight line (180°).
Reflex angle: take two arms from A and mark the angle the long way round, past the straight line, so it is more than 180°.
Mark each angle with a curve at A, and check by laying a square corner and a straight edge on it.
Put the centre of the protractor on the vertex T and the 0 line along the arm TP, then read the scale where each arm crosses it.
TR reads 30° and TQ reads 60°, so ∠PTR = 30° and ∠PTQ = 60°; both are less than 90°, so both are acute.
TW reads 102°, so ∠PTW = 102°, which is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
∠WTP has the same arms but goes the long way round, so ∠WTP = 360° − 102° = 258°.
Check: ∠PTW + ∠WTP = 102° + 258° = 360°, a full turn, and 258° is more than 180°, so ∠WTP is reflex.
Compare each measure with 90° and 180°: 140° is obtuse; 82°, 70° and 35° are acute; 195° is more than 180°, so it is reflex.
For 140°, 82°, 70° and 35°: put the centre of the protractor on the end of the base ray, count from 0 on the base ray, mark a dot at the measure and join it to the vertex.
195° is past the end of the scale (180°), so take it from the full turn: 360° − 195° = 165°.
Draw an angle of 165° with the scale, then mark the angle on the other side, the long way round; that outside angle is 195°.
Check: 165° + 195° = 360°, a full turn.
Sample answer: estimate each angle by eye first. Lay a square corner (90°) and a straight edge (180°) on it and see whether the opening is smaller, about equal or bigger.

Measure: put the centre of the protractor on the vertex, lay the 0 line along one arm and read the scale where the other arm crosses it. If the angle goes past a straight line, read the smaller side and take it from 360°.
Name the kind by comparing the measure with 90° and 180°: less than 90° is acute, 90° is right, more than 90° and less than 180° is obtuse, and more than 180° is reflex.
Check that each estimate is close to its measure and that the kind matches how the opening looks.
From the picture: angle a is acute, angles b and c are obtuse, angle d is acute, angle e is about a right angle (or slightly obtuse) and angle f is reflex.
